name: Adam Smith
bio: Adam Smith was a Scottish philosopher and economist who is considered the father of modern economics and a principal architect of free-market capitalism. A key figure of the Scottish Enlightenment, he authored 'The Theory of Moral Sentiments' in 1759 and his seminal opus 'The Wealth of Nations' in 1776. His conceptual insights regarding the division of labor, voluntary trade, and the 'invisible hand' of market forces laid the groundwork for modern macroeconomic theory.

famousWorks.title: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations
Formulation of the 'Invisible Hand' and division of labor principles

awards: Fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh (1783)
Lord Rector of the University of Glasgow (1787)
Depicted on the Bank of England £20 note (2007–2020)

faq.q: What is the 'Invisible Hand' concept introduced by Adam Smith?
faq.a: It describes the unseen market mechanism where individuals pursuing their own rational self-interest inadvertently promote the broader economic well-being and prosperity of society.

faq.q: What was the significance of the pin factory example in The Wealth of Nations?
faq.a: Smith used the manufacture of pins to demonstrate how the specialization and division of labor dramatically multiplies worker productivity and industrial efficiency.

name: John Maynard Keynes
bio: John Maynard Keynes, 1st Baron Keynes, was a British economist whose revolutionary ideas fundamentally changed the theory and practice of macroeconomics and the economic policies of governments. During the Great Depression of the 1930s, he spearheaded a revolution in economic thought that challenged classical economics, arguing that aggregate demand determines the overall level of economic activity and that government fiscal intervention is necessary during recessions. He was also a principal architect of the Bretton Woods system.

famousWorks.title: The Economic Consequences of the Peace
The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
Co-founding the Bretton Woods institutions (IMF and World Bank)

awards: Companion of the Order of the Bath (CB, 1917)
Time 100 Most Important People of the 20th Century

faq.q: What is the core premise of Keynesian economics?
faq.a: It posits that free markets lack self-balancing mechanisms that inevitably lead to full employment, justifying government deficit spending and fiscal stimulus during downturns to revive aggregate demand.

faq.q: What international institutions did Keynes help establish in 1944?
faq.a: At the Bretton Woods Conference in New Hampshire, Keynes served as a chief architect in establishing the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank.
